(10) On the single-person side: co-living operators and TOD micro-units in Jabodetabek are a thin analogue to China's studio-apartment economy, but the kos remains the dominant Indonesian format and has no Chinese equivalent.

HIGH confidence on: China's market size, pet population, spending structure and owner demographics (official White Paper series, consistent across Xinhua, China Daily, CCTV and USDA); China's demographic trajectory (NBS census and civil affairs data); China's regulatory and educational responses (documented, dated, primary-sourced); the qualitative mechanism linking household de-formation to pet spending; Indonesia's household composition (BPS Susenas), marriage decline (Kemenag SIMKAH), veterinarian shortage (PDHI), and the presence of specific Indonesian and Chinese players. MEDIUM confidence on: Indonesia's pet market size and growth rate (private market-research estimates only, with a 2x spread between sources and CAGR estimates ranging from 4.7% to 14.65%); the lag estimate, which is a reasoned construction from multiple partial indicators rather than a measured quantity. LOW confidence on: Indonesian pet ownership rates (three surveys give 52%, 67% and 72%), per-owner monthly spending (Rp 1.3-1.4m appears implausibly high as a national average), all Indonesian timeline projections beyond 2030, and any quantification of employment effects. The single-person-household half of this domain is analytically well-grounded but has far less Indonesian data than the pet half.
catatan_kontradiksi_data: (1) CHINA PET POPULATION DEFINITIONS CONFLICT. The White Paper series reports 126 million URBAN cats and dogs (2025); Goldman Sachs projects urban pets 'above 70 million' by 2030; USDA FAS projects 300 million TOTAL pets by 2035. These are not comparable — Goldman appears to use a narrower urban/household-verified definition, the White Paper counts urban cats and dogs only, and USDA counts all pets including rural dogs, birds, fish and reptiles. Any single 'China has X pets' claim should be treated as definition-dependent. (2) THE TASK BRIEF'S '300 MILLION PETS BY 2035' IS VERIFIED but sourced to USDA FAS GAIN reporting, not to Chinese official statistics, and it is a total-pet projection, not a projection of the urban dog-and-cat population that the RMB 312.6bn market figure covers. (3) MARKET SIZE UNIT ERRORS ARE ENDEMIC. Chinese sources report 3,126亿元 which is RMB 312.6 billion; multiple English secondary sources have mistranslated this as 3,126 billion or as USD figures at inconsistent exchange rates. One Xinhua-sourced English article states a 'projected 2025 market size of 811.4 billion yuan' — this refers to a broader pan-pet-industry definition (including production, exports and non-cat/dog animals), not the urban dog-and-cat consumption market, and the two are frequently conflated. (4) INDONESIA PET OWNERSHIP RATE VARIES BY 20 PERCENTAGE POINTS ACROSS SOURCES: Euromonitor/FMI ~67%, Rakuten Insight 2025 72%, JakPat 2026 52%. Online-panel surveys over-represent urban, higher-income, younger respondents; the BPS-derived series showing 4.80 million cats in 2022 is an order of magnitude lower because it counts a different thing. No reliable national pet census exists. (5) INDONESIA PET MARKET CAGR ESTIMATES RANGE FROM 4.69% (IMARC) TO 14.65% (6Wresearch) — a spread wide enough to make any 2030-2035 market-size figure unreliable; the USD 2.8bn (2025) to USD 6.8bn (2035) FMI path is used here as a mid-case, not a fact. (6) INDONESIA VETERINARIAN COUNT: PDHI membership ~13,500 versus 'around 20,000 licensed' in other reporting versus a stated need of ~70,000; the deficit is real and large but its exact size is not established. (7) INDONESIAN MARRIAGE DATA: BPS reports 1,478,302 marriages in 2024 (a decade low), while Kemenag SIMKAH data suggests a slight rebound to 1,479,533 in 2025 — the trend break is too recent to interpret and the two agencies use different registration bases (SIMKAH covers Muslim marriages via KUA; BPS aggregates including Dukcapil civil registration). (8) NEW RUIPENG'S LOSS FIGURE is reported in one source as 'nearly 40 billion RMB' over 2020-2022, which is implausibly large for a company of its revenue scale and is almost certainly a unit error for nearly RMB 4 billion (40亿); the corrected figure is used here. (9) China's one-person household figure of 125 million is from the 2020 census era; no more recent official update was located, so the current figure is likely higher.
